game.name: Inscryption
game.short_description: Inscryption is an inky black card-based odyssey that blends the deckbuilding roguelike, escape-room style puzzles, and psychological horror into a blood-laced smoothie. Darker still are the secrets inscrybed upon the cards...

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm gonna put this one as an easy s tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Inscryption is a story-driven deck-building roguelike from the creator of Pony Island. He treats it as the biggest campaign-style game on the list, something to experience once, and he avoids spoilers. He thinks the story, puzzles and exploration are superb and calls the game a masterpiece even though the card gameplay is its weakest part. He places it in S tier, close to Enter the Gungeon.
praise: Story and plot twists are absolutely amazing
Unusual mix of elements that combine very well
Puzzle elements and exploration with secrets to uncover
Works even for people who are not deck-building fans
Memorable one-time adventure that blew his mind
criticism: Card gameplay is the weakest part of the game
Not very well balanced, though he says it is not meant to be
unique_points: The most story-heavy campaign game on his list, hard to discuss without spoilers
A deck-builder that does not require deck-building expertise to enjoy
Mixes deck building, puzzles, exploration and narrative reveals
Designed to be played once, not replayed for hundreds of hours
commentary.quote: I'm gonna put this one as an easy s tier
design_criteria: Story and narrative: the main strength, with twists and secrets
Uniqueness of combinations: several genres blended effectively
Gameplay and balance: weakest aspect, easy to break and unbalanced
Puzzle and exploration: adds discovery beyond card battles
Replayability: meant to be played about once, unlike Gungeon
Accessibility: enjoyable without being a deck-building fan

community.one_liner: A deckbuilding roguelike from Daniel Mullins Games (published by Devolver Digital) that starts as a sacrifice-based card battler in a creepy cabin and keeps changing genre, blending escape-room puzzles, psychological horror and a meta-narrative across three acts.
community.consensus_summary: Inscryption is one of the best-reviewed indie games of 2021: Steam shows Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96.8% of roughly 149k reviews), Metacritic critics score it 85 with users at 8.5, and it swept major awards (GDC Game of the Year and the IGF Seumas McNally Grand Prize, a first for both). Praise centres on atmosphere, the blood/bones sacrifice card system, inventive puzzles and a story that constantly subverts expectations. The consistent dissent is that Act 1 is the peak: Acts 2 and 3 and the ARG-style meta-story are seen by a minority as a pacing drop, a bait-and-switch from the store page, or repetitive. It is a finished game (not early access); the free Kaycee's Mod (Mar 2022) added an endless roguelike mode, and it later shipped on Mac/Linux and consoles. Most players urge going in blind.
best_things: Act 1 atmosphere: the dark cabin, Leshy as a menacing card-game opponent, sound design and art style are repeatedly called one of a kind
Constant surprise: the game shifts genre, rules and format, and players say it is far more than the store page suggests
Sacrifice card system (blood, bones, scales) and sigils: easy to learn but with depth; the scale/tug-of-war damage mechanic was singled out by critics
Escape-room style puzzles and hidden secrets woven into the deckbuilding, with a stupid amount of detail according to players
Fourth-wall-breaking, meta storytelling and memorable characters (the four Scrybes); the ending handshake sequence is a fan favourite
Replay value: Kaycee's Mod gives an endless roguelike mode, plus challenges, achievements and ARG content; some players report hundreds of hours
Soundtrack and visual design: a twisted take on 90s floppy-disc adventure aesthetics (Eurogamer) and a well-loved OST
Teaches mechanics through play rather than tutorials, making it approachable even for people who dislike deckbuilders
worst_things: Many say the game peaks in Act 1; Act 2 (8-bit 2D) and Act 3 (sci-fi factory with P03) lose the horror tension and charm
Store page, trailer and demo show only Act 1, which a number of negative reviewers call a bait-and-switch
The meta-narrative / ARG (Karnoffel code, live-action video footage, real-world references) is called convoluted, hard to take seriously or not worth the time
Act 3 is seen by some as repetitive: map backtracking, many similar fights, and little downside to dying or save-scumming
Acts 2 and 3 are felt to have low stakes since the game is linear and failure barely sets you back, unlike Act 1
Tonal and mechanical whiplash: critics like PC Gamer said the eerie delight fades well before the end, and Destructoid said later chapters gripped less than the first
Overall length and pacing: some find the later parts a test of endurance with too many new mechanics introduced at once

The ending and overall story payoff disappoint some players: they expected branching outcomes or a stronger conclusion and felt the story was told shallowly or through a forgettable live-action framing
improvements: Make Act 1 (the most loved part) longer or offer more content in that format, or a stand-alone mode built around it (Kaycee's Mod was the partial answer)
Fully fleshed-out worlds and playable stories for Magnificus and Grimora, which fans say feel underdeveloped compared with Leshy and P03
Make Acts 2 and 3 carry real consequences for failure, and trim repetitive map traversal and filler fights in Act 3
Market the game more accurately, since store screenshots and trailers only show Act 1
Clearer or more optional delivery of the lore; some reviewers wanted the story told more directly rather than through ARG-style puzzles
Allow more player agency or alternate endings; some players expected branching outcomes that do not exist
unique_things: A deckbuilder wrapped in a horror escape room: you get up from the table, inspect the cabin and solve puzzles that change your cards and rules
Sacrifice-based costs (blood, bones, energy, gems) on a lane-based board with a scale for damage instead of player health
Each act is effectively a different game with a different look and card economy, all framed by a fictional 'game within a game' mystery
Meta-narrative that reaches outside the game (file manipulation, live-action footage, ARG codes, callbacks to Mullins' earlier games)
Grew from a Ludum Dare 43 prototype (Sacrifices Must Be Made) and won both GDC Game of the Year and the IGF Grand Prize, a first
tedious_or_disliked: Act 3's travel-fight-upgrade loop over a map, with back and forth between areas and many similar battles
Act 2 mechanics that feel underexplained or exploitable, leading some to ignore the puzzle of deck building
Decoding the ARG and Karnoffel code to understand the full story, which some find exhausting or unnecessary
divisive_points: The meta-story and ARG: fans call it brilliant and the reason to play; detractors call it a pretentious or creepypasta-like grab bag that hurts the game
Act 2: some love the puzzles and music, others call it the slog that kills the horror pacing
Whether Inscryption is a roguelike at all beyond Act 1 and Kaycee's Mod, versus a narrative puzzle game that uses deckbuilding
Replay value: Act 1 and Kaycee's Mod support replay, but the main story is linear and many consider it a one-time experience best played blind
community.reception_notes: Launched Oct 19, 2021 on Windows to strong reviews; Metacritic critic score 85 (49 critic reviews on the PC page; 1,107 user ratings) and user score 8.5. Won the GDC Game of the Year and IGF Seumas McNally Grand Prize (2022), plus a BAFTA for game design and many best-of-2021 lists. Wikipedia reports over 1 million copies sold by January 2022; a third-party Boxleiter-method estimate puts Steam owners at 2-5 million and gross revenue around 118M USD, which is an order-of-magnitude guess and not audited. Free Kaycee's Mod launched Mar 17, 2022. Platform releases: Linux/macOS Jun 2022, PS4/PS5 Aug 2022, Switch Dec 2022, Xbox Apr 2023. Not early access; no notable abandonment or controversy found. OpenCritic score could not be retrieved (the direct page and API were unavailable) so it is left null. Web search quota was exhausted, so community themes draw mainly on Steam reviews plus Metacritic and Wikipedia.
